PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation remains centred on Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA obligations for electronic monitoring and disconnecting from work, the 25-employee trigger, and whether the duty persists once triggered or is assessed on current headcount on the operative dates.

Trigger / timing points that recur:
* Electronic monitoring is tied to the 1 January 2022 snapshot for the first compliance year; employers 25+ on that date had to have a written policy by the spring 2022 effective date and provide it on hire and within 30 days of change. The majority view is the duty persists through the compliance year even if headcount later falls below 25.
* Disconnecting from work is tied to 1 July 2022 for the initial cohort, with employers 25+ on 1 January 2022 needing a policy by 2 June 2022. Employers reaching 25 after the reference date get ~3 months. A minority reads the duty as assessed on current headcount on 1 July 2022 / 1 January 2023.
* Distribution duty only attaches where a statutory policy is required; a purely voluntary policy for a <25 employer does not create an ESA breach.

Employer-by-employer current positions:

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and through 2022; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. Headcount is 20 <25 on 2 Jan 2023. 25+ threshold only reached on 10 Jan 2023 → three month start-up window. Unanimously compliant on assessment date.

B. 23 employees. <25 on both 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022 snapshots. No statutory duty to have or distribute a disconnecting or electronic-monitoring policy. Voluntary policies since 2020/2021 create no ESA distribution obligation. Refusing to distribute a voluntary policy is not a breach. Unanimously compliant.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → –2 Aug 2022 → –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023. 6 hires start 15 Feb 2023 → 24. Never 25+ on relevant reference dates. No statutory policy obligation as at 2 Jan 2023. Unanimously compliant.

C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022 → 25+ on both reference dates. Written disconnecting and electronic-monitoring policies exist and were initially distributed. Disagreement is on maintenance/distribution:
- Majority D camp: monthly updates with quarterly distribution is reasonable/arguable for a 1,000-person workforce and the statute does not mandate intra-month circulation; the employer is in substance covered.
- Minority C camp: ESA requires an updated policy within 30 days of a change; monthly changes with quarterly distribution can create 60-90 day lag, constituting ongoing non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 → electronic-monitoring obligation triggered for 2022 compliance year; disconnecting obligation triggered by 1 Jan 2022 25+ class. Employer has written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy but never developed a written electronic-monitoring policy. Headcount fell to 24 on 15 Mar 2022 and stayed there.
- Majority view: 1 Jan 2022 25+ snapshot fixes electronic-monitoring duty; later drop below 25 does not retroactively extinguish the duty already triggered. Missing electronic-monitoring policy is a continuing breach on 2 Jan 2023.
- Minority current-headcount view: on 1 July 2022 and on 1 Jan 2023 the employer has 24 employees <25, so neither disconnecting nor electronic-monitoring statutory duties are engaged on the operative dates; disconnect policy is voluntary and employer is compliant. reflection_text.3:
The deliberation is about ESA Working for Workers disconnecting-from-work and electronic/online monitoring policy duties assessed on 2 Jan 2023.

Key facts retained:
* A: 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022, still 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires effective/start 10 Jan 2023. No disconnect policy developed.
* B: 23 employees on assessment date; written disconnect policy since 2020 and written online monitoring policy since late 2021, but refuses distribution to new hires on cost grounds.
* C: ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Written and initially distributed both disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. Policies are amended monthly and a copy of the updated version is provided to each employee every fiscal quarter.
* D: 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees, no further change. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed.
* E: 22 employees on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023. 6 hires start 15 Feb 2023 → 24. No disconnect policy developed.

Threshold / timing points in play:
* Disconnect from work in force 1 Jul 2022 for 25+ employers; employers <25 on 1 Jul 2022 get until 2 Jun 2023 if they later reach 25+.
* Electronic monitoring in force 1 Jan 2023 for 25+ employers; many colleagues invoke 1 Jan 2022 snapshot for the initial compliance cohort with a three-month start-up window for employers who first reach 25 after that date.
* Distribution duty for both regimes: policy must be given to employees within 30 days of hire and an updated version must be given within 30 days of a change.

Competing answers and arguments from round 2:
D as non-compliant, majority position:
* 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 triggers electronic monitoring for the 2022/2023 compliance year and the disconnect cohort. Duty to have written policy attaches on that 1 Jan 2022 snapshot and is argued to persist even after headcount falls to 24 on 15 Mar 2022. The statute contains no “subsequent drop cures breach” provision.
* D has a disconnect policy but never developed an electronic monitoring policy. Missing electronic monitoring policy is a continuing breach as at 2 Jan 2023. The later fall to 24 does not retroactively extinguish the policy obligation triggered on 1 Jan 2022. Classic 25-employee snapshot / obligation-persists trap.
* A, B, E never meet the 25-employee reference date on the assessment date; prospective hires on 10 Jan 2023 and 15 Feb 2023 do not create a current duty. B’s voluntary policies create no ESA distribution duty for a <25 employer.
* C’s monthly internal revisions followed by quarterly circulation is treated as acceptable operational practice for a ~1,000-employee workforce; nothing mandates real-time/intra-month distribution.

C as non-compliant, minority position:
* Only C is 25+ on operative dates under a current-headcount reading: >25 on 1 Jul 2022 and >25 on 1 Jan 2023. A, B, D and E are <25 on the operative dates on that reading.
* C has written policies and initial distribution, but monthly amendment with quarterly provision means employees can operate 60-90 days under a superseded version. That is a failure to provide an updated policy within the statutory 30-day window, ongoing non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023.
* D’s 1 Jan 2022 30-employee count only fixes phase-in timing; after the drop to 24 on 15 Mar 2022 the employer is <25 on 1 Jul 2022 and on 1 Jan 2023, so neither mandatory disconnect nor electronic monitoring is engaged on 2 Jan 2023.

Disagreements and open issues:
* Snapshot vs current headcount for electronic monitoring: majority in round 2 treat obligation as triggered by 1 Jan 2022 headcount and continuing after fall below 25; minority treats test as current headcount on 1 Jan/2 Jan 2023.
* Effective dates: some cite electronic monitoring in force 1 Jan 2022 / spring 2022, others 1 Nov 2022 / 1 Jan 2023. Disconnect dates quoted as 2 Jun 2022 vs 1 Jul 2022.
* C distribution timing: is quarterly provision after monthly amendment a breach of 30-day-on-change or reasonable practice for large employer?
* Whether a voluntary policy imposes a statutory distribution duty for a <25 employer – consensus is no.

Belief update:
Prior best read favoured C on a strict current-headcount interpretation because only C is 25+ on 2 Jan 2023 and its monthly-update/quarterly-distribution practice breaches the 30-day update rule. Round 2 majority pushes the snapshot-trigger interpretation, making D the clear non-compliance for lacking a mandatory electronic monitoring policy triggered by 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and never developed, even though headcount is now 24. The C distribution-timing defect remains the most robust non-compliance under a strict current-headcount reading; the D defect is the most robust under a 1 Jan 2022 snapshot-persists reading. The unresolved nuance of the precise proclamation date for electronic monitoring and whether the duty is extinguished by a later drop below 25 remains the pivot between C and D.

Dispute is the maintenance/distribution timing: monthly internal amendments with copy to each employee only every fiscal quarter. Minority Colleagues 2,6,8 read the ESA requirement to give an updated copy within 30 days of a change as breached by a 60-90 day lag. Majority Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,7,9 read quarterly circulation for a ~1,000-person workforce as reasonable operational practice that satisfies “provide on change” and note nothing in O. Minority current-headcount reading, Colleagues 2,6,8: the operative test after phase-in is 25+ employees on the operative dates, 1 July 2022 for disconnecting and 1 Nov/1 Jan 2023 for electronic monitoring. D is 24 on both operative dates, so neither mandatory policy is engaged on 2 Jan 2023; the 1 Jan 2022 head-count only fixes phase-in timing. Under that reading D is compliant and C’s 30-day-on-change distribution lag is the only breach.

reflection_text.4:
The deliberation remains centred on Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA obligations for electronic monitoring and disconnecting from work, the 25-employee trigger, and whether the duty persists once triggered or is assessed on current headcount on the operative dates.

Trigger / timing points that recur:
* Electronic monitoring is tied to the 1 January 2022 snapshot for the first compliance year; employers 25+ on that date had to have a written policy by the spring 2022 effective date and provide it on hire and within 30 days of change. The majority view is the duty persists through the compliance year even if headcount later falls below 25.
* Disconnecting from work is tied to 1 July 2022 for the initial cohort, with employers 25+ on 1 January 2022 needing a policy by 2 June 2022. Employers reaching 25 after the reference date get ~3 months. A minority reads the duty as assessed on current headcount on 1 July 2022 / 1 January 2023.
* Distribution duty only attaches where a statutory policy is required; a purely voluntary policy for a <25 employer does not create an ESA breach.

Employer-by-employer current positions:

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and through 2022; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. Headcount is 20 <25 on 2 Jan 2023. 25+ threshold only reached on 10 Jan 2023 → three month start-up window. Unanimously compliant on assessment date.

B. 23 employees. <25 on both 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022 snapshots. No statutory duty to have or distribute a disconnecting or electronic-monitoring policy. Voluntary policies since 2020/2021 create no ESA distribution obligation. Refusing to distribute a voluntary policy is not a breach. Unanimously compliant.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → –2 Aug 2022 → –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023. 6 hires start 15 Feb 2023 → 24. Never 25+ on relevant reference dates. No statutory policy obligation as at 2 Jan 2023. Unanimously compliant.

C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022 → 25+ on both reference dates. Written disconnecting and electronic-monitoring policies exist and were initially distributed. Disagreement is on maintenance/distribution:
- Majority D camp: monthly updates with quarterly distribution is reasonable/arguable for a 1,000-person workforce and the statute does not mandate intra-month circulation; the employer is in substance covered.
- Minority C camp: ESA requires an updated policy within 30 days of a change; monthly changes with quarterly distribution can create 60-90 day lag, constituting ongoing non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 → electronic-monitoring obligation triggered for 2022 compliance year; disconnecting obligation triggered by 1 Jan 2022 25+ class. Employer has written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy but never developed a written electronic-monitoring policy. Headcount fell to 24 on 15 Mar 2022 and stayed there.
- Majority view: 1 Jan 2022 25+ snapshot fixes electronic-monitoring duty; later drop below 25 does not retroactively extinguish the duty already triggered. Missing electronic-monitoring policy is a continuing breach on 2 Jan 2023.
- Minority current-headcount view: on 1 July 2022 and on 1 Jan 2023 the employer has 24 employees <25, so neither disconnecting nor electronic-monitoring statutory duties are engaged on the operative dates; disconnect policy is voluntary and employer is compliant. This is the basis for the C-as-breach arguments.

Unresolved tension: persistence of the 1 Jan 2022 trigger vs a strict current-headcount assessment on operative dates, and the materiality of C’s monthly-update/quarterly-distribution practice under the 30-day update rule.

Weight of evidence in this round: 11 colleagues now explicitly endorse D as the non-compliant employer, citing the classic trigger-and-persist trap for electronic monitoring. 3 colleagues endorse C based on a current-headcount reading and the 30-day update distribution defect. Colleague 13 explicitly endorses the snapshot-trigger reading and rejects the C timing breach as overstated.

Current best belief: Employer D is not in compliance as of 2 Jan 2023 for lack of the mandatory electronic-monitoring policy triggered by its 30-employee headcount on 1 Jan 2022, the duty not being cured by the subsequent fall to 24. The C distribution timing issue remains the principal counter-argument, but the statutory persistence of the 1 Jan 2022 electronic-monitoring trigger is the more decisive and majority-supported basis.

The continuing obligations are to have a written policy and to give each employee a copy on hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change to the policy.
* Electronic/online monitoring – ESA s.64.0.1 / O.Reg.311/22. The regulation applies to an employer who employs 25 or more employees in Ontario on the operative date. The policy must be given to each employee on hire and an updated copy must be given within 30 days of a change.

Application on the assessment date 2 January 2023

A – 20 employees on 1 January 2022 and 20 employees on 2 January 2023. The eight agreements with an effective/start date of 10 January 2023 do not exist on 2 January 2023. <25 on the operative dates for both regimes; no mandatory disconnecting or electronic-monitoring duty is engaged on the assessment date. The prospective 28-employee head-count will only start a three-month clock from 10 January 2023.

B – 23 employees on 2 January 2023. <25 on 1 July 2022 and on the electronic monitoring operative date. The statutory disconnecting and electronic-monitoring duties are not engaged. The 2020 disconnecting policy and the late-2021 online monitoring policy are purely voluntary for a <25 employer; a refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach.

D – 30 on 1 January 2022, 30-6 = 24 after the 15 March 2022 terminations and unchanged thereafter. 24 employees on 1 July 2022 and 24 employees on 2 January 2023. <25 on both operative dates, so neither a mandatory disconnecting-from-work nor a mandatory electronic-monitoring policy is required on 2 January 2023. The disconnecting policy D holds is therefore voluntary on the assessment date and the absence of a written electronic-monitoring policy is not a statutory breach because the electronic-monitoring regime is not engaged for a 24-employee employer on 2 January 2023.

E – 22 on 1 January 2022, –2 resignations August 2022 →20, –2 retirements 31 December 2022 →18 employees on 2 January 2023. Six hires starting 15 February 2023 give a projected 24 employees. <25 on the reference dates and on 2 January 2023; no statutory policy duty is triggered on the assessment date.

C is ≥25 throughout the whole period – ≈1,000 employees on 1 January 2022 and 987-1,012 at all points in 2022 – so it is a covered employer for both regimes on 1 July 2022 and on 1 January 2023 and it does have written disconnecting-from-work and electronic-monitoring policies that were initially distributed.

The continuing compliance duty for a 25+ employer is the maintenance/distribution duty. An updated policy must be provided to each employee within 30 days of a change to the policy. C amends both the disconnecting-from-work and electronic-monitoring policies every month but only provides a copy of the updated policies to each employee every fiscal quarter. An employee can therefore be working for 60-90 days under a superseded version of the policy without having received the statutory update. That is a failure to give an updated policy within the 30-day-on-change window and is an ongoing non-compliance with the provision and distribution obligation for a 25+ employer as at 2 January 2023.

A, B, D and E are below the 25-employee operative threshold on 2 January 2023 and are not required to have a mandatory disconnecting-from-work or electronic-monitoring policy on that date. C is the only employer in the set that is a covered employer on the assessment date and is in breach of the 30-day-on-change distribution requirement.

The assessment date is 2 January 2023. The two Working for Workers duties in force are the right-to-disconnect duty, ESA s.64.1 / O.Reg.224/22, and the electronic/online monitoring duty, ESA s.64.0.1 / O.Reg.311/22. 

Both regimes fix the first 25+ compliance cohort by the 1 January 2022 head-count snapshot. An employer who employed 25 or more employees in Ontario on 1 January 2022 is in the initial class for the 2022-2023 cycle. The duty to have a written policy in place for that cycle attaches on that snapshot and the regulations contain no “subsequent reduction cures the duty” language. The continuing obligations for a covered employer are to have the written policy and to give a copy on hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change.

* A – 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 agreements with effective/start 10 Jan 2023 do not exist on the assessment date. <25 on every statutory reference date. No mandatory disconnect or electronic monitoring duty is engaged on 2 Jan 2023. The prospective 28 head-count will only start a three-month start-up clock on 10 Jan 2023.

* B – 23 employees on the assessment date. <25 on 1 Jan 2022 and on 1 July 2022. The statutory disconnect and electronic monitoring duties are not engaged. The 2020 disconnecting and late 2021 online monitoring documents are voluntary; a <25 employer has no ESA distribution duty for a voluntary policy.

* E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022, –2 retirements eff. 31 Dec 2022 = 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 give a projected 24. <25 on the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot and on 2 Jan 2023. No statutory policy duty is triggered on the assessment date.

* C – c.1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. 25+ on the 1 Jan 2022 electronic monitoring snapshot and on the 1 July 2022 disconnect snapshot and remains ≥25 on 2 Jan 2023. Written disconnecting-from-work and electronic-monitoring policies are in place and were initially distributed. Monthly internal revision with quarterly circulation to a ~1,000-person workforce is an administrable practice for satisfying the “provide an updated copy within 30 days of a change” requirement; the substantive written-policy requirement is met on the assessment date.

* D – 30 employees on 1 January 2022. That 1 January 2022 25+ head-count triggers the electronic-monitoring obligation for the 2022/2023 compliance period and the initial disconnecting-from-work class.

30 – 6 terminations 15 March 2022 = 24 employees thereafter and unchanged. 24 on 1 July 2022 and 24 on 2 January 2023.

The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, satisfying the disconnect duty that was triggered. It has never developed a written electronic-monitoring policy at all. The later fall to 24 does not retroactively extinguish the electronic-monitoring duty that attached on 1 January 2022 when the employer was a 30-employee employer. The missing mandatory electronic-monitoring policy is a continuing breach as at 2 January 2023.

That is the classic 25-employee snapshot / obligation-persists trap. D is the only employer that was in the 25+ class on the statutory reference date and remains without the required mandatory policy on the assessment date.

C

On 2 January 2023 the two Working for Workers policy duties in force are

* Right to disconnect, ESA s.64.1 / O.Reg.224/22 – a written policy is required for an employer who employs 25 or more employees in Ontario. An employer who was 25+ on 1 January 2022 had to be compliant by 2 June 2022; an employer who first reaches 25 after that date has a three-month start-up window. Provision on hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change is required.
* Electronic/online monitoring, ESA s.64.0.1 / O.Reg.311/22 – a written policy is required for an employer who employs 25 or more employees in Ontario on the operative date. The initial phase-in class is identified by the 1 January 2022 head-count for timing purposes, but the ongoing test is current size. Provision on hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change is required.

Head-count on the assessment date

* A – 20 employees on 1 January 2022 and 20 on 2 January 2023. The 8 agreements effective/start 10 January 2023 do not exist on the assessment date. <25 on every statutory reference date; no mandatory disconnect or electronic monitoring duty is engaged on 2 January 2023.
* B – 23 employees on 2 January 2023. <25 on 1 January 2022/1 July 2022 and on the electronic monitoring operative date. The statutory duties are not engaged. The 2020/2021 disconnecting and online monitoring documents are voluntary for a <25 employer; a refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach.
* D – 30 on 1 January 2022, 30-6 = 24 after 15 March 2022 and unchanged. 24 employees on 1 July 2022 and 24 on 2 January 2023. <25 on both operative dates on the assessment date, so neither a mandatory disconnecting-from-work nor a mandatory electronic-monitoring policy is required on 2 January 2023. The disconnecting policy D holds is voluntary on the assessment date.
* E – 22 on 1 January 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022, –2 retirements 31 December 2022 = 18 employees on 2 January 2023; six hires starting 15 February 2023 give a projected 24. <25 on the reference dates and on 2 January 2023; no statutory policy duty is triggered.

C is a covered employer throughout. c.1,000 employees on 1 January 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022, i.e. ≥25 on 1 July 2022 and ≥25 on the electronic monitoring commencement date. It does have written disconnecting-from-work and electronic-monitoring policies and performed the initial distribution.

The continuing maintenance obligation for a 25+ employer is to give each employee a copy of the policy on hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change to the policy. C amends both policies every month but only circulates a copy of the updated policies to each employee every fiscal quarter. An employee can therefore be working for 60-90 days under a superseded version of the policy without having received the statutory update. That is a failure to provide an updated policy within 30 days of a change and is an ongoing non-compliance with the provision and distribution obligation for a 25+ employer as at 2 January 2023.

A, B, D and E are below the 25-employee operative threshold on 2 January 2023 and are not required to have a mandatory disconnecting-from-work or electronic-monitoring policy on that date. C is the only employer in the set that is a covered employer on the assessment date and is in breach of the 30-day-on-change distribution requirement.

D

The 1 January 2022 snapshot under O. Reg. 311/22 fixes the initial 25+ cohort for the electronic-monitoring obligation, and the regulation contains no language that would allow a later head-count reduction to extinguish an already-triggered duty. Employer D crossed that threshold at 30 employees, so the requirement to maintain a written electronic-monitoring policy attached for the 2022–2023 compliance period and remains in force on 2 January 2023 regardless of the March 2022 drop to 24. The complete absence of any such policy is therefore a continuing breach.

Colleagues 2, 6 and 8 correctly observe that D’s current head-count places it below 25 on the 2023 operative date, yet that reading would render the statutory reference-date mechanism surplusage. The regulation’s text ties the first-year class expressly to the 1 January 2022 count, and once that class is engaged the duty to have the policy in place persists for the compliance year. No “current-size only” override appears in either O. Reg. 311/22 or the parallel disconnecting-from-work provisions.

By contrast, C remains a 25+ employer on every relevant snapshot, already holds both required written policies, and performed the initial distribution. Its monthly internal revisions followed by quarterly circulation to a 1 000-employee workforce satisfies the “provide updated copy within 30 days of a change” obligation; nothing in the text imposes intra-month or real-time distribution for a large workforce. Employers A, B and E never met any 25-employee reference-date test, so no statutory policy duty was ever engaged. The only employer whose facts produce an ongoing, unexcused breach of a triggered obligation is therefore D.

* Electronic monitoring is tied to the 1 January 2022 snapshot for the first compliance cohort; employers 25+ on that date had to have a written policy by the spring 2022 effective date and provide it on hire and within 30 days of change. * Electronic monitoring is tied to the 1 January 2022 snapshot for the first compliance cohort; employers 25+ on that date had to have a written policy by the spring 2022 effective date and provide it on hire and within 30 days of change. Majority view is the duty persists through the compliance year even if headcount later falls below 25.
* Disconnecting from work is tied to 1 July 2022 for initial cohort, with employers 25+ on 1 January 2022 needing policy by 2 June 2022. Employers reaching 25 after reference date get ~3 months.
* Distribution duty only attaches where a statutory policy is required; a purely voluntary policy for a <25 employer does not create ESA breach.

Employer-by-employer current positions:

A. 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and through 2022; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023 → headcount 20 <25 on 2 Jan 2023. Threshold only reached 10 Jan 2023 → three month start-up. Unanimously compliant on assessment date.

B. 23 employees. <25 on both 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022 snapshots. No statutory duty to have/distribute disconnecting or electronic-monitoring policy. Voluntary policies since 2020/2021 create no ESA distribution obligation. Refusing to distribute voluntary policy is not a breach. Unanimously compliant.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → –2 Aug 2022 → –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023. 6 hires start 15 Feb 2023 → 24. Never 25+ on relevant reference dates. No statutory policy obligation as at 2 Jan 2023. Unanimously compliant.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 → electronic-monitoring obligation triggered for 2022 compliance year; disconnecting obligation triggered by 1 Jan 2022 25+ class.
